claim: The prelimbic region or Area 32 (A32) in Paxinos and Watson, 2014, of the medial PFC is needed to initially acquire goal-directed actions and learn the relationship between distinct actions and their outcomes.
source: Specifically, the prelimbic region or Area 32 (A32) in Paxinos and Watson, 2014, of the medial PFC is needed to initially acquire goal-directed actions and learn the relationship between distinct actions and their outcomes (Hart et al., 2018; Killcross and Coutureau, 2003; Tran-Tu-Yen et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Hart et al., 2018; Killcross and Coutureau, 2003; Tran-Tu-Yen et al., 2009) that provide evidence for this role of the prelimbic region.

claim: The gustatory region of the insular cortex is required to recall the current value of outcomes to guide choice between competing actions.
source: whereas the gustatory region of the insular cortex is required to recall the current value of these outcomes to guide choice between competing actions (Balleine and Dickinson, 2000; Parkes and Balleine, 2013; Parkes et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Balleine and Dickinson, 2000; Parkes and Balleine, 2013; Parkes et al., 2015).

claim: The ventral (VO) and lateral (LO) subregions of the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) are required for goal-directed actions.
source: In addition, the ventral (VO) and lateral (LO) subregions of the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) are required for goal-directed actions (Gremel and Costa, 2013; Gremel et al., 2016; Zimmermann et al., 2017; Rhodes and Murray, 2013; Fiuzat et al., 2017; Malvaez et al., 2019; Sias et al., 2021; Wassum, 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Gremel and Costa, 2013; Gremel et al., 2016; Zimmermann et al., 2017; Rhodes and Murray, 2013; Fiuzat et al., 2017; Malvaez et al., 2019; Sias et al., 2021; Wassum, 2022).

claim: The ventral and lateral subregions of the OFC are required to update previously established instrumental associations.
source: specifically to update previously established instrumental associations (Parkes et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Parkes et al., 2018.

claim: Behavioural flexibility requires activity in noradrenergic (NA) neurons of the locus coeruleus (LC).
source: Behavioural flexibility also requires activity in noradrenergic (NA) neurons of the locus coeruleus (LC), which are thought to track uncertainty in the current situation (Bouret and Sara, 2004; Cope et al., 2019; Jahn et al., 2018; McGaughy et al., 2008; Tait et al., 2007; Tervo et al., 2014; Uematsu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Bouret and Sara, 2004; Cope et al., 2019; Jahn et al., 2018; McGaughy et al., 2008; Tait et al., 2007; Tervo et al., 2014; Uematsu et al., 2017).

claim: Noradrenergic neurons of the locus coeruleus are thought to track uncertainty in the current situation.
source: Behavioural flexibility also requires activity in noradrenergic (NA) neurons of the locus coeruleus (LC), which are thought to track uncertainty in the current situation (Bouret and Sara, 2004; Cope et al., 2019; Jahn et al., 2018; McGaughy et al., 2008; Tait et al., 2007; Tervo et al., 2014; Uematsu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Bouret and Sara, 2004; Cope et al., 2019; Jahn et al., 2018; McGaughy et al., 2008; Tait et al., 2007; Tervo et al., 2014; Uematsu et al., 2017).

claim: Theoretical models hypothesize that the LC interacts with the PFC to support behavioural flexibility.
source: Most notably, compelling theoretical models hypothesize that the LC interacts with the PFC to support behavioural flexibility (Sara and Bouret, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sara and Bouret, 2012.

claim: SAP infusion resulted in extensive NA fibres loss in the VO and LO.
source: SAP infusion resulted in extensive NA fibres loss in the VO and LO, as revealed by a main effect of group (F(1,53) = 277.33, p<0.001) and region (F(1,53) = 12.25, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data (F-statistics and p-values) and is also shown in Figure 1C.

claim: NA fibres volume was greater in the VO compared to LO for the CTL group.
source: simple effect analyses revealed that NA fibres volume was greater in the VO compared to LO for the CTL group (F(1,53) = 23.38, p<0.001), a result consistent with previous findings (Cerpa et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-statistic and p-value) and is consistent with previous findings cited (Cerpa et al., 2019). The data is also shown in Figure 1C.

claim: All rats acquired the lever pressing response, with their rate of lever pressing increasing across days.
source: As shown in Figure 1D, all rats acquired the lever pressing response, with their rate of lever pressing increasing across days (F(1,53) = 508.30, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-statistic and p-value) and is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: All groups showed sensitivity to the change in outcome value during the outcome devaluation test, indicating that rats learned the A-O associations and the current value of the outcomes.
source: All groups also showed sensitivity to the change in outcome value during the outcome devaluation test, indicating that rats learned the A-O associations and the current value of the outcomes, that is, goal-directed behaviour was intact (Figure 1E). Indeed, we found a significant effect of devaluation (Ndev vs. Dev; F(1,53) = 79.62, p<0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-statistic and p-value) and is shown in Figure 1E.

claim: NA depletion in PFC regions does not affect the initial learning or expression of goal-directed actions.
source: Thus, NA depletion in PFC regions does not appear to affect the initial learning or expression of goal-directed actions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing no differences between control and SAP groups in initial training and testing.

claim: Performance increased across reversal training days.
source: We found that performance increased across reversal training days (F(1,53) = 22.73, p<0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-statistic and p-value) and is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The CTL groups reduced their responding on the action associated with the devalued outcome, while NA-depleted animals did not.
source: While the CTL groups reduced their responding on the action associated with the devalued outcome, NA-depleted animals did not. Statistical analyses confirmed this observation revealing no main effects of group, treatment, or devaluation (all F(1,53) values <2.89, p-values >0.10), and no significant devaluation × group interaction (F(1,53) = 0.007, p=0.93). However, there was a significant devaluation × treatment interaction (F(1,53) = 5.00, p<0.05) and simple effect analyses confirmed that the CTL groups biased their responding toward the lever associated with the non-devalued outcome (F(1,53) = 7.35, p<0.01), while rats in the depleted groups did not (F(1,53) = 0.15, p=0.70).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-statistics and p-values) and is shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Depletion of NA innervation to the OFC and other prefrontal regions renders rats unable to associate new outcomes to acquired actions.
source: These results show that depletion of NA innervation to the OFC and other prefrontal regions renders rats unable to associate new outcomes to acquired actions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing impaired reversal learning in NA-depleted animals.

claim: This deficit was present in rats that received NA depletion before (group Pre) and after (group Post) learning the initial A-O associations.
source: Importantly, this deficit was present in rats that received NA depletion before (group Pre) and after (group Post) learning the initial A-O associations.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design and results showing similar deficits in both Pre and Post groups.

claim: 6-OHDA infusion resulted in fewer TH-positive fibres in the OFC.
source: In the OFC, we found a significant within-subject effect of region (VO vs. LO; F(1,26) = 8.17, p<0.01) and fewer TH-positive fibres in the 6-OHDA group (n=12), as compared to the CTL (n=8) and 6-OHDA+Desi (n=9) groups (F(1,26) = 41.14, p<0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-statistics and p-values) and is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 6-OHDA induced a significant reduction in the volume of NA fibres in both the VO and the LO.
source: simple effect analyses revealed that 6-OHDA induced a significant reduction in the volume of NA fibres in both the VO (F(1,26) = 400.75, p<0.001) and the LO (F(1,26) = 459.37, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-statistics and p-values) and is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Rats with 6-OHDA infusions responded more during reversal training than the CTL.
source: We found that rats with 6-OHDA infusions (n=12) responded more during reversal training than the CTL (n=8; F(1,18) = 14.74, p<0.01) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-statistic and p-value) and is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CTL rats successfully adjusted their behaviour according to the new A-O contingencies, but the 6-OHDA group did not.
source: During the outcome devaluation test following reversal training (Figure 3C), CTL rats successfully adjusted their behaviour according to the new A-O contingencies, but the 6-OHDA group did not. Statistical analysis revealed no main effect of group (F(1,18) < 0.001, p>0.975), but a main effect of devaluation (F(1,18) = 8.72, p<0.01) and a group × devaluation interaction that approached statistical significance (F(1,18) = 3.90, p=0.06). Simple effect analyses confirmed that CTL rats responded more on the lever associated with the devalued outcome (F(1,18) = 10.12, p<0.01), while 6-OHDA rats did not show this preference (F(1,18) = 0.6, p=0.45).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-statistics and p-values) and is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both the 6-OHDA+Desi and CTL groups showed goal-directed behaviour and biased their choice towards the action associated with the non-devalued outcome.
source: Moreover, we found that both groups showed goal-directed behaviour and biased their choice towards the action associated with the non-devalued outcome (Figure 3E). Statistical analyses confirmed a main effect of devaluation (F(1,15) = 5.25, p<0.05), but no main effect of group (F(1,15) < 0.001, p>0.975) or group × devaluation interaction (F(1,15) = 0.17, p=0.69).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-statistics and p-values) and is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Full CA depletion (DA + NA) in the OFC, A32, and M2 impairs performance in an outcome-identity reversal task, while depletion restricted to DA innervation leaves performance intact.
source: We show that full CA depletion (DA + NA) in the OFC, A32, and M2 impairs performance in an outcome-identity reversal task, while depletion restricted to DA innervation leaves performance intact.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results comparing 6-OHDA and 6-OHDA+Desi groups.

claim: Injection of anti-DHβ SAP or 6-OHDA in the OFC caused a significant reduction of fibres in other regions of the PFC.
source: However, injection of anti-DHβ SAP or 6-OHDA in the OFC also caused a significant reduction of fibres in other regions of the PFC, most likely because of NA fibres crossing the OFC before entering these other prefrontal regions (Chandler and Waterhouse, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Chandler and Waterhouse, 2012 explaining the mechanism.

claim: CAV2 vectors are readily taken up at presynapse and trafficked via retrograde transport to the soma of projecting neurons.
source: CAV2 vectors are readily taken up at presynapse and trafficked via retrograde transport to the soma of projecting neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about CAV2 vectors.

claim: mCherry staining is present at injection sites, reflecting local cortico-cortical connections that are not NA dependent.
source: As expected, while mCherry staining is present at injection sites, reflecting local cortico-cortical connections that are not NA dependent (Figure 4B), HA-immunoreactive cell bodies were found exclusively in the LC (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4B and is based on inference about the nature of local connections.

claim: HA-immunoreactive cell bodies were found exclusively in the LC.
source: As expected, while mCherry staining is present at injection sites, reflecting local cortico-cortical connections that are not NA dependent (Figure 4B), HA-immunoreactive cell bodies were found exclusively in the LC (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The data are consistent with NA-specific expression of the HA-tagged hM4Di due to PRS, and nonselective expression of mCherry which is under the control of hSyn.
source: These data are consistent with NA-specific expression of the HA-tagged hM4Di due to PRS, and nonselective expression of mCherry which is under the control of hSyn.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations about the distribution of HA and mCherry staining.

claim: Only the CTL group (-/-) showed goal-directed behaviour and performed the action associated with the non-devalued outcome more than the action associated with the devalued outcome.
source: For rats injected in the OFC (Figure 5C), we found that only the CTL group (-/-) showed goal-directed behaviour and performed the action associated with the non-devalued outcome more than the action associated with the devalued outcome. By contrast, rats with bilateral LC:vlOFC NA projections silenced during the reversal training (+/-), or the outcome devaluation test (-/+), or during both phases (+/+) failed to display this preference in responding. Statistical analyses confirmed no significant between- or within-subject main effects (largest F(1,46) value = 1.22, p=0.28), but a significant three-way interaction (devaluation × treatment during acquisition × treatment during test: F(1,23) = 5.45, p<0.05). Simple effects analyses confirmed that only rats that received vehicle during both training and test (-/-) biased their choice towards the lever associated with the non-devalued outcome (F(1,23) = 7.10, p<0.05), while rats in the -/+ (F(1,23) = 0.09, p=0.77), +/- (F(1,23) = 1.93, p=0.18), and +/+ conditions (F(1,23) = 0.01, p=0.92) did not.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-statistics and p-values) and is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Silencing LC:A32 NA projections left goal-directed behaviour intact.
source: By contrast, silencing LC:A32 NA projections left goal-directed behaviour intact (Figure 5E). Indeed, we found a main effect of devaluation (F(1,15) = 5.76, p<0.05), but no effect of treatment during acquisition (F(1,15) = 0.35, p=0.56) or treatment during test (F(1,15) = 0.53, p=0.47), and no significant interactions between these factors (largest F(1,15) value = 1.62, p-values > 0.21).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-statistics and p-values) and is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: LC NA projections to the OFC, but not to A32, are required to both encode and recall changes in the identity of the expected outcome.
source: Together, these results indicate that LC NA projections to the OFC, but not to A32, are required to both encode and recall changes in the identity of the expected outcome.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results comparing LC:vlOFC and LC:A32 silencing.

claim: NA inputs to the OFC are an essential component of the updating process for goal-directed actions.
source: Our data demonstrate that NA inputs to the OFC might be an essential component of this updating process.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the overall experimental results.

claim: Animals with a loss of NA inputs in the OFC can initially learn and express A-O contingencies, but are impaired when the identity of the outcome has been modified.
source: First, we demonstrated that animals with a loss of NA inputs in the OFC can initially learn and express A-O contingencies, but are impaired when the identity of the outcome has been modified.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental results from the SAP experiment.

claim: Such deficits were also observed when NA depletion occurred immediately before the encoding of the new A-O contingencies.
source: Importantly, such deficits were also observed when NA depletion occurred immediately before the encoding of the new A-O contingencies.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental results from the Post group in the SAP experiment.

claim: Combined depletions of DA and NA, but not of DA alone, induced a profound deficit in outcome reversal.
source: We then showed that this impairment was selective to NA inputs, because combined depletions of DA and NA, but not of DA alone, induced a profound deficit in outcome reversal.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental results from the 6-OHDA experiments.

claim: Silencing LC:vlOFC, but not LC:A32, projections impaired the rats' ability to acquire and express the reversed instrumental contingencies.
source: We found that silencing LC:vlOFC, but not LC:A32, projections impaired the rats' ability to acquire and express the reversed instrumental contingencies.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental results from the chemogenetic experiments.

claim: The use of the SAP toxin led to a dramatic decrease of NA fibres density in all analysed cortical areas.
source: The use of the SAP toxin led to a dramatic decrease of NA fibres density in all analysed cortical areas (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Injection of 6-OHDA led to less offsite NA depletion compared to SAP.
source: However, injection of 6-OHDA led to less offsite NA depletion suggesting that a large part of the previous observation is toxin-specific.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental results between SAP and 6-OHDA experiments.

claim: No significant loss of NA fibres was visible in the insula cortex following 6-OHDA injection.
source: Indeed, no significant loss of NA fibres was visible in the insula cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), which has been previously implicated in goal-directed behaviour (Balleine and Dickinson, 2000; Parkes and Balleine, 2013; Parkes et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and citations to studies on the role of insula in goal-directed behaviour.

claim: LC cells mainly target a single region, and only a small proportion of LC neurons collateralize to minor targets.
source: These studies, using various techniques, indicate that LC cells mainly target a single region, and that only a small proportion of LC neurons collateralize to minor targets (Plummer et al., 2020; Kebschull et al., 2016; Uematsu et al., 2017; Chandler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Plummer et al., 2020; Kebschull et al., 2016; Uematsu et al., 2017; Chandler et al., 2014).

claim: The OFC NA innervation is presumably specific.
source: Therefore, even if the OFC NA innervation is presumably specific (Chandler et al., 2013), we cannot rule out a possible collateralization of some neurons toward neighbouring prefrontal areas (including A32 and MO).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chandler et al., 2013.

claim: The posterior ventral portion of the OFC is an entry point for LC fibres en passant, which ultimately target other prefrontal areas.
source: We have previously discussed that the posterior ventral portion of the OFC is an entry point for LC fibres en passant, which ultimately target other prefrontal areas (Cerpa et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cerpa et al., 2019.

claim: The CAV2 vector can infect axons-of-passage, however the vector does not spread more than 200 µm from the injection site.
source: It has been shown that the CAV2 vector can infect axons-of-passage, however the vector does not spread more than 200 µm from the injection site (Schwarz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schwarz et al., 2015.

claim: The current behavioural results are in line with previous work showing that the ability to associate new outcomes to previously acquired actions is impaired following chemogenetic inhibition of the VO and LO.
source: Overall, the current behavioural results are in line with our previous work showing that the ability to associate new outcomes to previously acquired actions is impaired following chemogenetic inhibition of the VO and LO (Parkes et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Parkes et al., 2018.

claim: The ability to associate new outcomes to previously acquired actions is impaired following disconnection of the VO and LO from the submedius thalamic nucleus.
source: or disconnection of the VO and LO from the submedius thalamic nucleus (Fresno et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fresno et al., 2019.

claim: Different subregions of the OFC, both along the medio-lateral and antero-posterior axes of OFC, display clear functional heterogeneities.
source: However, it is worth mentioning that different subregions of the OFC, both along the medio-lateral and antero-posterior axes of OFC, display clear functional heterogeneities (Bradfield and Hart, 2020; Izquierdo, 2017; Panayi and Killcross, 2018; Bradfield et al., 2018; Barreiros et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Bradfield and Hart, 2020; Izquierdo, 2017; Panayi and Killcross, 2018; Bradfield et al., 2018; Barreiros et al., 2021).

claim: The LC displays some anatomical and physiological variations between male and female rats.
source: The LC displays some anatomical and physiological variations between male and female rats (Joshi and Chandler, 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Joshi and Chandler, 2020.

claim: NA inputs to the OFC are required for both the encoding and the recall of new A-O associations.
source: In addition, chemogenetic silencing of the LC:vlOFC pathway before the reversal training, or before testing also produced similar impairments, which further demonstrates that OFC NA inputs are required for both the encoding and the recall of new A-O associations.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental results from the chemogenetic experiments.

claim: NA inputs to A32 (the prelimbic cortex) are not required for responding based on initial or reversed instrumental contingencies.
source: In contrast to NA inputs to the OFC, our results show that NA inputs to A32 (the prelimbic cortex) are not required for responding based on initial or reversed instrumental contingencies.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental results from the chemogenetic experiments targeting LC:A32.

claim: NA inputs to the medial wall of the PFC are required for attentional regulation.
source: Indeed, NA inputs to the medial wall of the PFC are required for attentional regulation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Lesioning NA inputs or chemogenetic inhibition of NA inputs to the mPFC alters attentional set-shifting.
source: Specifically, lesioning NA inputs (McGaughy et al., 2008; Newman et al., 2008) or chemogenetic inhibition of NA inputs to the mPFC (Cope et al., 2019) alters attentional set-shifting
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (McGaughy et al., 2008; Newman et al., 2008; Cope et al., 2019).

claim: NA recapture inhibition via atomoxetine improves attentional set-shifting.
source: while NA recapture inhibition via atomoxetine improves it (Newman et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Newman et al., 2008.

claim: OFC NA depletion can alter cue-outcome reversal, but not dimensional shift, in an attentional set-shifting task.
source: OFC NA depletion can also alter cue-outcome reversal, but not dimensional shift, in an attentional set-shifting task (Mokler et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mokler et al., 2017.

claim: Reversible inactivation of the medial OFC (mOFC) decreased performance accuracy on a two-armed bandit task in rats.
source: Recently, it was also shown that reversible inactivation of the medial OFC (mOFC) decreased performance accuracy on a two-armed bandit task in rats (Swanson et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Swanson et al., 2022.

claim: Performance accuracy on a two-armed bandit task was impaired following systemic, but not intra-mOFC, administration of an NA antagonist.
source: Interestingly, performance accuracy was also impaired following systemic, but not intra-mOFC, administration of an NA antagonist (Swanson et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Swanson et al., 2022.

claim: DA signalling in the prelimbic cortex/A32 plays a critical role in the detection of contingency degradation.
source: The role of cortical DA-dependent mechanisms in goal-directed behaviour remains poorly understood, but we have previously shown that DA signalling in the prelimbic cortex/A32 plays a critical role in the detection of contingency degradation (Naneix et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Naneix et al., 2009.

claim: Detection of contingency degradation is likely to involve the processing of non-expected rewards which induces, at the level of A32, a DA-dependent reward prediction error signal.
source: Such detection is likely to involve the processing of non-expected rewards which induces, at the level of A32, a DA-dependent reward prediction error signal (Montague et al., 2004; Schultz and Dickinson, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Montague et al., 2004 and Schultz and Dickinson, 2000.

claim: Some have reported impaired adaptation to contingency changes following inhibition of VO and LO or BDNF knockdown in these regions.
source: Some have reported impaired adaptation to contingency changes following inhibition of VO and LO or BDNF knockdown in these regions (Whyte et al., 2021; Zimmermann et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Whyte et al., 2021 and Zimmermann et al., 2017.

claim: Inhibition of VO/LO leaves sensitivity to degradation intact, at least during an initial test.
source: while another study showed that inhibition of VO/LO leaves sensitivity to degradation intact, at least during an initial test (Zimmermann et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zimmermann et al., 2018.

claim: Inactivation of anterior OFC (Area 11) in marmosets improves instrumental contingency degradation, whereas overactivation impairs degradation.
source: Interestingly, a recent paper in marmosets demonstrates that inactivation of anterior OFC (Area 11) improves instrumental contingency degradation, whereas overactivation impairs degradation (Duan et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Duan et al., 2021.

claim: When trained on reversed contingencies, animals encode the new A-O associations.
source: When trained on reversed contingencies, animals encode the new A-O associations (Fresno et al., 2019; Parkes et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fresno et al., 2019 and Parkes et al., 2018.

claim: Reversal learning performance is the result of updating prior existing A-O contingencies without unlearning the initial contingencies.
source: Under similar experimental conditions, past research has shown that reversal learning performance is the result of updating prior existing A-O contingencies without unlearning the initial contingencies (Bradfield and Balleine, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bradfield and Balleine, 2017.

claim: The animals build a partition between a state for the new contingencies and the initial state of old contingencies.
source: In other words, the animals build a partition between a state for the new contingencies and the initial state of old contingencies (Hart and Balleine, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hart and Balleine, 2016.

claim: The OFC is critically involved in the partition of information when task states change without explicit notice.
source: Current research has proposed that the OFC is critically involved in this partition of information when task states change without explicit notice (McDannald et al., 2011; Wilson et al., 2014; Sadacca et al., 2017, Wikenheiser and Schoenbaum, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (McDannald et al., 2011; Wilson et al., 2014; Sadacca et al., 2017, Wikenheiser and Schoenbaum, 2016).

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of the OFC (ventral and lateral) impairs goal-directed responding following identity reversal.
source: Consistent with this view, chemogenetic inhibition of the OFC (ventral and lateral) impairs goal-directed responding following identity reversal (Parkes et al., 2018; Howard and Kahnt, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Parkes et al., 2018 and Howard and Kahnt, 2021.

claim: A rise in NA activity allows for behavioural flexibility when a change in contingencies is detected.
source: Such a proposal is in accordance with popular LC-NA system theories suggesting that a rise in NA activity allows for behavioural flexibility when a change in contingencies is detected (Aston-Jones et al., 1997; Bouret and Sara, 2005; Sadacca et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Aston-Jones et al., 1997; Bouret and Sara, 2005; Sadacca et al., 2017).

claim: DCZ significantly decreased the percentage of hM4Di/c-Fos-positive cells following stress.
source: Most importantly, DCZ significantly decreased the percentage of hM4Di/c-Fos-positive cells following stress (≈35% decrease), as revealed by a significant Student's t-test (p=0.034).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test and p-value) and is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The stress procedure resulted in a fivefold increase in c-Fos expression in the LC.
source: As expected, the stress procedure resulted in a fivefold increase in c-Fos expression in the LC.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A total of 136 male Long-Evans rats, aged 2–3 months, were obtained from the Centre d'Elevage Janvier (France).
source: A total of 136 male Long-Evans rats, aged 2–3 months, were obtained from the Centre d'Elevage Janvier (France).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: Rats were housed in pairs with ad libitum access to water and standard lab chow prior to behavioural experiments.
source: Rats were housed in pairs with ad libitum access to water and standard lab chow prior to behavioural experiments.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the housing conditions.

claim: The experiments received approval from the local Bordeaux Ethics Committee (CE50).
source: The experiments received approval from the local Bordeaux Ethics Committee (CE50).
evidence: This is a factual statement about ethical approval.
